question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

ALACRITY
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Eagerness.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alacrity (noun) means brisk and cheerful readiness; a prompt willingness to act. (तत्परता, उत्साह)
◦ Example: The volunteers accepted the extra duty with alacrity.

 

• Eagerness carries the same sense — keen and willing enthusiasm to do something. (उत्सुकता)
◦ Example: She answered the summons with an eagerness that surprised the committee.

 

• Note that alacrity combines two ideas at once — speed and willingness. A person may act quickly out of fear, but that is not alacrity; the word requires that the promptness be cheerful.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Reluctance (अनिच्छा): unwillingness or hesitation to do something — the direct opposite of alacrity.

 

• Option 3: Hesitation (संकोच): a pause caused by doubt or unwillingness — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Sluggishness (सुस्ती): slowness and lack of energy — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the design: three antonyms and one synonym. Fix the meaning of the given word first, then discard every option that agrees with the majority sense.

 

• Other synonyms of alacrity: promptness, willingness, readiness, avidity, zeal.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To put a spoke in someone's wheel
option_1: To obstruct or hinder someone's plans
option_2: To repair a vehicle damaged in an accident
option_3: To take charge of a task that others have abandoned
option_4: To speak on someone's behalf at a meeting
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To obstruct or hinder someone's plans.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "To put a spoke in someone's wheel" means to create a deliberate obstacle in the way of another person's plan or progress. (किसी के काम में रोड़ा अटकाना)
◦ Example: A single objection from the finance wing put a spoke in the department's wheel.

 

• The image comes from the old practice of thrusting a pin or bar into the wheel of a cart to stop it from turning on a slope. The action is intentional, which is why the idiom always carries a note of blame.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the idiom literally as vehicle repair — the standard trap in idiom questions.

 

• Option 3 describes taking on abandoned work, nearer to "to pick up the pieces".

 

• Option 4 describes advocacy, for which the idiom would be "to put in a word for someone".

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of obstruction: "To throw a spanner in the works", "To throw cold water on" (to discourage a plan), "To stand in someone's way" and "To pull the rug from under someone's feet".

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

PROLIFIC
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Unproductive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prolific (adjective) means producing much fruit, offspring or work; highly productive. It is used of writers, artists, plants and animals alike. (बहुप्रसवी, बहुत उपजाऊ)
◦ Example: He was the most prolific writer of his generation, with forty novels to his name.

 

• Its true opposite is unproductive — not producing or able to produce much. (अनुत्पादक)
◦ Example: The soil in that stretch is thin and largely unproductive.

 

• The word comes from Latin proles (offspring) + facere (to make) — the same root as proletariat, which originally meant those whose only contribution to the state was their children.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Fertile (उपजाऊ): capable of producing abundant growth — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Fruitful (फलदायी): producing good results in plenty — also a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Abundant (प्रचुर): existing in large quantity — again close in sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of prolific: barren, sterile, infertile, meagre, sparse.

 

• Do not confuse prolific (productive) with profligate (recklessly extravagant) — a pair SSC has set against each other more than once.

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sacreligious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Sacrilegious" — showing disrespect towards something regarded as sacred. (पवित्रता का अपमान करने वाला)
◦ Example: Removing the inscription was condemned as a sacrilegious act.

 

• Spelling key: SAC + RI + LEG + IOUS. The trap is powerful because the word looks as though it came from "religious" — but it does not. It comes from sacrilege, which is from Latin sacer (sacred) + legere (to gather, to steal). The i and the e are therefore in the opposite order from religious.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Ubiquitous (सर्वव्यापी) — correctly spelt; present everywhere at once.

 

• Option 2: Perspicuous (स्पष्ट) — correctly spelt; clearly expressed and easy to understand.

 

• Option 4: Innocuous (हानिरहित) — correctly spelt; harmless and inoffensive. Note the double n at the start and the single c: in-noc-uous.

 

NOTE

 

• Other words whose spelling misleads because of a false resemblance: pronunciation (not pronounciation, though the verb is pronounce), maintenance (not maintainance, though the verb is maintain), and exaggerate (double g, single r).

question: Spot the correct spelling of the laboratory technique used to separate the components of a mixture.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Chromatography.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Chromatography" is the technique of separating the components of a mixture by passing it in solution or suspension through a medium in which the components move at different rates. (वर्णलेखन)
◦ Example: Paper chromatography separated the pigments present in the leaf extract.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: CHROMA (colour) + GRAPHY (writing, recording) — literally colour writing, because the method was first used to separate coloured plant pigments.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Cromatography" — incorrect; the "h" after the initial c has been dropped.

 

• Option 3: "Chromotography" — incorrect; the root is "chroma", not "chromo", in this word.

 

• Option 4: "Chromatograpy" — incorrect; the suffix is "-graphy", with an h.

 

NOTE

 

• Other words built on the chroma root: chromosome (so named because it takes up stain readily), monochrome (one colour), polychrome (many colours) and achromatic (without colour).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A person who falsely claims to possess special knowledge or skill'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Charlatan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A charlatan is a person who pretends to expertise he does not have, especially in order to deceive others for gain. (ठग, पाखंडी)
◦ Example: The tribunal described the so-called consultant as a charlatan.

 

• The essential element is deliberate pretence. A charlatan is not merely mistaken; he knows he lacks the knowledge he claims.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Sycophant (चाटुकार): one who flatters a powerful person in order to gain advantage.

 

• Option 2: Renegade (दलबदलू, विश्वासघाती): one who deserts a cause, party or faith for another.

 

• Option 4: Dilettante (शौकिया): one who dabbles in an art or subject for amusement, without serious study. This is the closest trap — but a dilettante makes no false claim to expertise, which is what distinguishes him from a charlatan.

 

NOTE

 

• Related one-word substitutes: Quack (an untrained person practising medicine), Impostor (one who assumes a false identity), Hypocrite (one who feigns virtue) and Plagiarist (one who passes off another's work as his own).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The inaugural function was called ___ after the audit revealed large discrepancies in the accounts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. off.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrasal verb "call off" means to cancel a planned event or to abandon something already under way. (रद्द करना)
◦ Example: The search was called off after three days.

 

• The context settles it: discrepancies discovered in an audit would lead to the cancellation of the function, not to any of the other senses.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "call out" — to shout, or to summon someone into action (the army was called out).

 

• Option 3: "call for" — to demand or require (the situation calls for restraint), or to collect someone on the way.

 

• Option 4: "call on" — to pay a short visit, or to formally request someone to speak.

 

NOTE

 

• A single verb can change meaning entirely with the particle, which is why SSC favours these questions. Note the family built on put: put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), put down (suppress, or write), put forward (propose) and put out (extinguish, or inconvenience).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The archivist was plainly reluctant to part ___ the original manuscripts even for a week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Part with" means to give up possession of something, usually with reluctance. The preposition is fixed and cannot be varied. (छोड़ना, सौंपना)
◦ Example: She could not bear to part with her father's books.

 

• Distinguish it carefully from "part from", which means to separate from a person: He parted from his colleagues at the gate. The rule is easy to remember — part with things, part from people.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: from — correct English, but it would mean separating from a person, not surrendering an object.

 

• Option 2: of — not used with part in this sense.

 

• Option 4: off — no such phrasal verb exists.

 

NOTE

 

• Other verbs whose meaning turns on the preposition: agree with a person / agree to a proposal; wait for someone / wait on a customer; differ from a thing / differ with a person; compare to (to liken) / compare with (to examine side by side).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The officials who had cleared the proposal were conspicuously ___ from the review meeting that followed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. absent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Conspicuously absent" is a fixed collocation meaning noticeably and pointedly not present, in a way that itself invites comment. (स्पष्ट रूप से अनुपस्थित)
◦ Example: Any mention of the earlier report was conspicuously absent from the minutes.

 

• The phrase carries an implication: the absence is not accidental but significant. That is exactly the sense the sentence requires, since the officials who cleared the proposal might have been expected to attend its review.

 

• Note also that "absent from" takes the preposition from, which the sentence already supplies.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: away — would take from but does not collocate with conspicuously, and suggests merely being elsewhere.

 

• Option 2: missing — suggests something lost or unaccounted for, which does not suit people who chose not to attend.

 

• Option 3: lacking — used of qualities that are wanting (lacking in confidence), not of people not present.

 

NOTE

 

• Adverb–adjective collocations regularly tested by SSC: conspicuously absent, diametrically opposed, mutually exclusive, patently false, blissfully unaware, eminently suitable and manifestly unjust.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The dispute was finally settled (1)/ between the contractor and I (2)/ after the arbitrator (3)/ examined all the records. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of pronoun case. "Between" is a preposition, and a preposition is always followed by the objective case of the pronoun — me, not I.

◦ Corrected sentence: The dispute was finally settled between the contractor and me after the arbitrator examined all the records.

 

• The simplest test is to drop the other noun: nobody would write settled between I. The presence of the contractor and does not change the case required.

 

• The mistake is common because and I is drilled into learners as the polite form. It is correct only when the pair is the subject: The contractor and I signed the agreement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the simple past passive was settled is well formed.

 

• Part (3) is correct — after the arbitrator is a properly formed subordinate clause opening.

 

• Part (4) is correct — the simple past examined suits the sequence of events.

 

NOTE

 

• The same rule governs let, like, between, but (meaning except) and all other prepositions: Let him and me go; No one but her knew; between you and me. Use the subject forms I, he, she, we, they only when the pronoun performs the action.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Scarcely had the minister (1)/ finished his address (2)/ than the audience began to leave (3)/ the hall in large numbers. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Scarcely" is always completed by "when", never by than.

◦ Corrected sentence: Scarcely had the minister finished his address when the audience began to leave the hall in large numbers.

 

• The two structures are close in meaning but their partners are fixed and must not be mixed:

◦ Hardly / Scarcely / Barely … when
◦ No sooner … than

 

• Note that the inversion in part (1) is correct. Because the sentence opens with the negative adverb Scarcely, the auxiliary rightly precedes the subject — Scarcely had the minister finished.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the inversion after Scarcely is properly formed.

 

• Part (2) is correct — the past perfect had finished rightly marks the earlier of the two actions.

 

• Part (4) is correct — in large numbers is a well-formed adverbial phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• In all three structures the earlier action takes the past perfect and the later one the simple past: No sooner had he sat down than the bell rang. Remember also that hardly, scarcely and barely are already negative and must never be paired with another negative.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The department will announce the revised schedule next week.
option_1: The revised schedule is announced by the department next week.
option_2: The revised schedule will announce by the department next week.
option_3: The revised schedule would be announced by the department next week.
option_4: The revised schedule will be announced by the department next week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The revised schedule will be announced by the department next week.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Simple Future Tense — structure: will + V1.

 

• The passive of the simple future is formed as: Object + will be + V3 + by + Subject.

◦ Active: The department will announce the revised schedule.
◦ Passive: The revised schedule will be announced by the department.

 

• The word "be" is essential. After a modal such as will, the passive always takes modal + be + V3, never the modal followed directly by the participle.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses "is announced", the passive of the simple present, which clashes with next week.

 

• Option 2 omits "be", leaving an active form with a passive agent — the schedule appears to be doing the announcing.

 

• Option 3 uses "would be", shifting the sentence into the conditional or reported past.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive forms of the future group: Simple Future → will be + V3; Future Perfect → will have been + V3. The Future Continuous and the Future Perfect Continuous have no passive form in ordinary use.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The report will have been submitted by the committee before the last date.
option_1: The committee will have submitted the report before the last date.
option_2: The committee will submit the report before the last date.
option_3: The committee has submitted the report before the last date.
option_4: The committee had submitted the report before the last date.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The committee will have submitted the report before the last date.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Future Perfect Passive — structure: will have been + V3. Its active counterpart is the Future Perfect Active — will have + V3.

◦ Passive: The report will have been submitted by the committee.
◦ Active: The committee will have submitted the report.

 

• The agent after "by" becomes the subject, the original subject becomes the object, and the tense must be carried over unchanged. The future perfect is required because the action will be completed before a stated future point — here, the last date.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses the simple future, which loses the sense of completion before a deadline.

 

• Option 3 uses the present perfect, wrongly placing a future action in the past.

 

• Option 4 uses the past perfect, which pushes the action further back still.

 

NOTE

 

• The future perfect is signalled by phrases such as by tomorrow, by next month, before the deadline and by the time you arrive. Whenever such a phrase appears, check that the tense has survived the conversion intact.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The auditor was discreet about the irregularities he had come across.
option_1: The officer was discreet in making his enquiries.
option_2: She remained discreet about the whole affair.
option_3: A discreet word to the manager settled the matter.
option_4: The syllabus is divided into six discrete modules.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The syllabus is divided into six discrete modules.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Discreet means careful and tactful in speech and action, so as to avoid causing offence or revealing private matters.
• Discrete means separate and individually distinct. The two are pronounced alike, so "discrete" is the homophone required.

◦ Example: The data were grouped into discrete categories with no overlap.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all reuse the same spelling "discreet" in the sense of tactful, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: in discrete, the two es are separated by the t — just as discrete things are separate.

 

• Note the noun forms, which differ sharply: discretion from discreet, and discreteness from discrete.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

When India launched its Pulse Polio Immunisation programme in 1995, the country accounted for a substantial share of all the polio cases reported anywhere in the world. Two decades later it was certified free of the disease. The interval between those two facts is often described as a triumph of medicine, which is only half true. The vaccine had existed since the 1950s; what had to be invented was a way of delivering it to every child in a country of that size.

 

The method that finally worked was repetition on a scale no other campaign had attempted. Instead of relying on routine immunisation alone, the programme set aside national immunisation days on which every child under five was to be given drops, whether or not the child had received them before. Millions of volunteers were mobilised, houses were marked in chalk, and teams returned to the ones they had missed. Migrant families at railway stations, brick kilns and construction sites — the group most likely to be overlooked — were sought out separately.

 

The hardest obstacle was not logistical. In several districts the campaign met deep resistance, fed by rumours about the vaccine's purpose and by the memory of health services that had been unreliable in every other respect. Persuasion, where it succeeded, came less from officials than from local religious leaders, schoolteachers and mothers who had already vaccinated their own children.

 

The last case was reported from West Bengal in January 2011, and certification followed in March 2014. What the episode is usually taken to prove is that India can execute at scale. The more useful lesson is narrower and harder: that a programme reaches the last few per cent only when it stops treating them as a residue and begins treating them as its principal task.

 

What was the name of the programme launched by India in 1995?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The Pulse Polio Immunisation programme.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The opening sentence names it directly: India launched its Pulse Polio Immunisation programme in 1995, at a time when the country accounted for a substantial share of all polio cases reported anywhere in the world.

 

• The passage supplies three dates, each attached to a different event. Keeping them apart is the whole task here:

◦ 1995 — the programme is launched.
◦ January 2011 — the last case is reported.
◦ March 2014 — certification follows.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 3 and 4 name real programmes, but none of them appears anywhere in the passage.

 

• Distractors of this kind — genuine names drawn from the same field — are the standard SSC trap in questions about a named scheme. Only what the passage states can be the answer.

 

NOTE

 

• Questions naming a scheme, body or programme are pure location questions: the answer is a proper noun sitting in the text. Find the sentence containing the date and the name is almost always in the same clause.

What, according to the passage, was distinctive about the method that finally worked?
option_1: It relied on a newly developed vaccine
option_2: It concentrated resources on the worst-affected districts alone
option_3: It repeated the dose on national immunisation days regardless of earlier doses
option_4: It replaced volunteers with trained medical staff
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. It repeated the dose on national immunisation days regardless of earlier doses.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The second paragraph describes the method as repetition on a scale no other campaign had attempted: national immunisation days on which every child under five was to be given drops, whether or not the child had received them before.

 

• The author stresses that this was an organisational innovation, not a medical one. The opening paragraph makes the same point — the vaccine had existed since the 1950s; what had to be invented was a way of delivering it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 contradicts the passage, which states that the vaccine was already decades old.

 

• Option 2 reverses the design — the campaign deliberately sought out the most easily overlooked groups, such as migrant families at railway stations and brick kilns.

 

• Option 4 is contradicted by the reference to millions of volunteers.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage opens by rejecting the obvious explanation — here, "which is only half true" — the real explanation almost always follows in the next paragraph, and a question is usually built on it.

What does the author identify as the hardest obstacle faced by the campaign?
option_1: Resistance fed by rumours and by the memory of unreliable health services
option_2: The difficulty of transporting the vaccine in hot weather
option_3: A persistent shortage of trained volunteers
option_4: Disagreement between the central and state governments
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Resistance fed by rumours and by the memory of unreliable health services.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph opens by ruling out the obvious answer — the hardest obstacle was not logistical — and then names the real one: deep resistance in several districts, fed by rumours about the vaccine's purpose and by the memory of health services that had been unreliable in every other respect.

 

• The second half of that explanation is the author's sharpest point. The suspicion was not irrational; it rested on people's actual experience of the health system, which is why persuasion had to come from those they already trusted.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 2 and 3 are both logistical difficulties, which the passage expressly sets aside.

 

• Option 4 introduces centre–state friction, a subject the passage never raises.

 

NOTE

 

• The construction "The hardest obstacle was not X" guarantees two things: that X will appear as a distractor, and that the real answer follows immediately. Read one sentence further before choosing.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. local religious leaders, schoolteachers and mothers.

• The passage states that persuasion, where it succeeded, came less from officials than from local religious leaders, schoolteachers and mothers who had already vaccinated their own children.

 

• The last clause matters. What convinced people was not an argument but an example — a neighbour who had already accepted the risk on behalf of her own child.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 names the group the passage explicitly ranks lower — officials — in the phrase less from officials than from.

 

• Options 1 and 3 introduce advertising and financial incentives, neither of which appears in the passage.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch the construction "less from X than from Y". It is a comparison, not a denial, and the answer is always Y. SSC reliably builds a distractor out of X, as Option 2 shows.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

When India launched its Pulse Polio Immunisation programme in 1995, the country accounted for a substantial share of all the polio cases reported anywhere in the world. Two decades later it was certified free of the disease. The interval between those two facts is often described as a triumph of medicine, which is only half true. The vaccine had existed since the 1950s; what had to be invented was a way of delivering it to every child in a country of that size.

 

The method that finally worked was repetition on a scale no other campaign had attempted. Instead of relying on routine immunisation alone, the programme set aside national immunisation days on which every child under five was to be given drops, whether or not the child had received them before. Millions of volunteers were mobilised, houses were marked in chalk, and teams returned to the ones they had missed. Migrant families at railway stations, brick kilns and construction sites — the group most likely to be overlooked — were sought out separately.

 

The hardest obstacle was not logistical. In several districts the campaign met deep resistance, fed by rumours about the vaccine's purpose and by the memory of health services that had been unreliable in every other respect. Persuasion, where it succeeded, came less from officials than from local religious leaders, schoolteachers and mothers who had already vaccinated their own children.

 

The last case was reported from West Bengal in January 2011, and certification followed in March 2014. What the episode is usually taken to prove is that India can execute at scale. The more useful lesson is narrower and harder: that a programme reaches the last few per cent only when it stops treating them as a residue and begins treating them as its principal task.

 

What does the author call the more useful lesson of the episode?
option_1: That India is capable of executing programmes at very large scale
option_2: That a programme succeeds only when it treats the hardest few per cent as its principal task
option_3: That vaccines should be developed within the country rather than imported
option_4: That volunteers are more effective than trained officials in every field
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That a programme succeeds only when it treats the hardest few per cent as its principal task.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The closing sentence states it in as many words: the more useful lesson is that a programme reaches the last few per cent only when it stops treating them as a residue and begins treating them as its principal task.

 

• The author sets this against the popular reading of the episode — that India can execute at scale — and calls his own lesson narrower and harder. The whole passage supports it: the chalk marks on houses, the return visits, and the separate search for migrant families were all directed at the hardest fraction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the interpretation the author sets aside as less useful.

 

• Option 3 raises domestic vaccine production, which the passage does not discuss.

 

• Option 4 generalises one feature of a single campaign into a rule about every field.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence of the form "What this is usually taken to prove is X. The more useful lesson is Y." is the clearest possible signal of a central-idea question, and the answer is always Y.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

She is fully capable to handle the entire section on her own.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. capable of handling.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective "capable" is always followed by "of" + gerund, never by an infinitive.

◦ Corrected sentence: She is fully capable of handling the entire section on her own.
◦ Example: The machine is capable of printing four hundred pages an hour.

 

• Since "of" is a preposition, the verb after it must take the gerund (V + ing) form. Writing capable of handle would be as wrong as capable to handle.

 

• Compare the adjective "able", which takes the opposite pattern — able + to + V1: She is able to handle the section. The two adjectives are close in meaning but their structures are fixed and opposite.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "capable to handling" mixes an infinitive marker with a gerund.

 

• Option 2: "capable for handling" uses the wrong preposition.

 

• Option 4 repeats the original error.

 

NOTE

 

• Adjectives followed by of + gerund: capable of, desirous of, confident of, afraid of, fond of, tired of, incapable of and guilty of. Adjectives followed by to + V1: able to, liable to, likely to, eager to, anxious to and reluctant to.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

His approach to the problem is entirely different than the one adopted last year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. different from.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective "different" is followed by "from" in standard English, not by than.

◦ Corrected sentence: His approach to the problem is entirely different from the one adopted last year.
◦ Example: The revised form is quite different from the old one.

 

• The error arises from confusing different with a comparative adjective. Words such as greater, better and higher take than, but different is not a comparative and therefore does not.

 

• The related verb takes the same preposition when things are compared: differ from. Note, however, that when people disagree, the verb takes with — I differ with you on this point.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original error.

 

• Option 3: "different to than" places two prepositions together and is impossible.

 

• Option 4: "differ from" substitutes a verb for the adjective, leaving the sentence with two finite verbs.

 

NOTE

 

• Other adjectives with fixed prepositions tested by SSC: similar to, identical with, married to, senior to, popular with, familiar with, angry with (a person), surprised at and indifferent to.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The convenor said to us, "Let us postpone the meeting till Monday."
option_1: The convenor proposed that we should postpone the meeting till Monday.
option_2: The convenor said that let us postpone the meeting till Monday.
option_3: The convenor told us to postpone the meeting till Monday.
option_4: The convenor asked whether we should postpone the meeting till Monday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The convenor proposed that we should postpone the meeting till Monday.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A sentence beginning with "Let us" expresses a proposal or suggestion addressed to a group that includes the speaker. Its rules of conversion are:

◦ The reporting verb becomes proposed or suggested.
◦ The conjunction "that" is added.
◦ "Let us" is replaced by "we should", since the speaker includes himself among those who will act.

 

• Applying these gives: proposed that we should postpone the meeting.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps "let us" inside a that-clause, so no conversion has taken place.

 

• Option 3 uses "told us to", which reports a command addressed to others and excludes the speaker — it corresponds to "Postpone the meeting," he said.

 

• Option 4 turns the proposal into a question, whose direct form would be "Shall we postpone the meeting?"

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the two "let" structures apart:
◦ "Let us" as a proposal → proposed/suggested that we should …
◦ "Let me / Let him" asking permission → requested that he might be allowed to …

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

He said that he was leaving that place the next morning.
option_1: "I was leaving that place the next morning," he said.
option_2: "I am leaving that place tomorrow morning," he said.
option_3: "He is leaving this place tomorrow morning," he said.
option_4: "I am leaving this place tomorrow morning," he said.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. "I am leaving this place tomorrow morning," he said.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Converting back to direct speech reverses every change made during the original conversion. Three of them apply here:

◦ Tense: was leaving is restored to "am leaving".
◦ Place word: that place is restored to "this place".
◦ Time word: the next morning is restored to "tomorrow morning".
◦ Pronoun: he becomes "I", since the speaker is now speaking for himself.

 

• Only Option 4 applies all four changes together.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 restores neither the tense nor the time and place words.

 

• Option 2 restores the tense and the time word but leaves "that place" unchanged.

 

• Option 3 keeps the third person "He" inside the quotation, so the speaker appears to be describing somebody else.

 

NOTE

 

• Reverse changes from indirect to direct speech: that day → today; the next day → tomorrow; the previous day → yesterday; then → now; there → here; that → this; those → these; and would → will, could → can, might → may, had to → must.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. Ramesh's barber shop opposite the district hospital has occupied the same room for twenty-six years.

 

A. He began writing names and blood groups on the back page of his appointment diary.

 

B. Patients' relatives often came in asking whether he knew anyone with a particular blood group.

 

C. By the third year the page had become a folded sheet carrying more than four hundred entries.

 

D. The hospital now telephones him before it telephones the blood bank.

 

S2. He still does not charge anybody for the calls he makes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-A-C-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – C – D – S2. The paragraph follows a situation → need → response → growth → outcome order.

 

• S1 establishes the situation — a shop of long standing opposite a hospital.

◦ B supplies the need that arose from that location: relatives asking about blood groups. It must come first, since nothing else explains why he would start a list.
◦ A is his response — writing the names down in his diary.
◦ C must follow A, because "the page" refers to the back page of the diary named there.
◦ D gives the outcome — the hospital now calls him first — and leads into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-C-D) has him start the list before anyone has asked for it.

 

• Option 2 (B-C-A-D) mentions "the page" before any page has been introduced.

 

• Option 4 (A-C-B-D) strands sentence B in the middle, where the need arises only after the list is complete.

 

NOTE

 

• The definite-article test settles this question by itself: a sentence opening with the + a noun not yet mentioned — here the page in C — can never come before the sentence that introduces it.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The Moon shows the same face to the Earth night after night, and has done so for most of its history.

 

A. Over a very long period that drag slowed the spin until the two periods matched exactly.

 

B. It turns on its own axis in precisely the time it takes to travel once around us.

 

C. The Earth's gravity raises a slight bulge in the Moon's rocky body, which drags against its rotation.

 

D. That coincidence is not a coincidence at all, and it has a straightforward mechanical cause.

 

S2. The same process has locked many other moons in the solar system to the planets they circle.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-D-C-A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – C – A – S2. The paragraph moves from observation → puzzle → mechanism → result.

 

• S1 states the observation — the Moon shows us one face.

◦ B explains what that means in terms of motion: its rotation period equals its orbital period. This must come first, because it is the fact that D calls a coincidence.
◦ D raises the puzzle — the match is not accidental — and promises a cause, so it must precede the explanation.
◦ C supplies the mechanism: the tidal bulge raised by the Earth's gravity, which drags against the Moon's rotation.
◦ A gives the result, and "that drag" refers straight back to the drag named in C.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (D-B-C-A) speaks of "that coincidence" before any coincidence has been described.

 

• Option 2 (B-C-D-A) gives the mechanism before the puzzle it is meant to solve, leaving D stranded.

 

• Option 4 (C-B-D-A) opens with the mechanism, so the reader is told the cause before learning what needs explaining.

 

NOTE

 

• Two demonstratives fix the entire order here without any knowledge of astronomy: "That coincidence" in D binds it to B, and "that drag" in A binds it to C. Tracking demonstratives is the single most reliable technique in rearrangement questions.
